arXiv:0912.2759v1 [math.PR] 14 Dec 2009

Improved mixing time bounds for the
Thorp shuffle

Ben Morris ††thanks: Department of Mathematics, University of California, Davis. Email: morris@math.ucdavis.edu. Research partially supported NSF grant DMS-0707144.
Abstract

E. Thorp introduced the following card shuffling model. Suppose the number of cards nn is even. Cut the deck into two equal piles. Drop the first card from the left pile or from the right pile according to the outcome of a fair coin flip. Then drop from the other pile. Continue this way until both piles are empty. We show that if nn is a power of 22 then the mixing time of the Thorp shuffle is O⁡(log3⁡n)O(\log^{3}n). Previously, the best known bound was O⁡(log4⁡n)O(\log^{4}n).

Key words: Markov chain, mixing time.

1 Introduction

Card shuffling has a rich history in mathematics, dating back to work of Markov [7] and Poincare [11]. A basic problem is to determine the mixing time, i.e., the number of shuffles necessary to mix up the deck (sec Section 3 for a precise definition). In [6], the author found a general method that reduces bounding the mixing time of a card shuffle to verifying a local condition that involves only pairs of cards. This was used to give mixing time bounds for the Thorp shuffle and Durrett’s LL-reversal chain. In the present paper, we build on the techniques of [6] and get an improved analysis of the Thorp shuffle.

2 Previous work

Thorp [13] introduced the following card shuffling model in 1973. Assume that the number of cards, nn, is even. Cut the deck into two equal piles. Drop the first card from the left pile or the right pile according to the outcome of a fair coin flip; then drop from the other pile. Continue this way, with independent coin flips deciding whether to drop left-right or right-left each time, until both piles are empty.

Analyzing the Thorp shuffle is an old problem with theoretical roots. However, recently the Thorp shuffle has found applications in applied cryptography. The author, Phil Rogaway and Till Stegers have used the Thorp shuffle as the basis for a practical algorithm for encoding small messages such as social security numbers and credit card numbers (see [9]). In order to analyze the algorithm it is important to have good bounds on the mixing time.

The Thorp shuffle, despite its simple description, has been hard to analyze. Determining its mixing time has been called the “longest-standing open card shuffling problem” [3]. In [10] the author obtained the first poly log upper bound, proving a bound of O⁡(log44⁡n)O(\log^{44}n), valid when nn is a power of 22. Montenegro and Tetali [8] built on this to get a bound of O⁡(log29⁡n)O(\log^{29}n). In [6] the bound was improved to O⁡(log4⁡n)O(\log^{4}n), with no power-of-two assumption. In the present paper we show that if the number of cards is a power of two, then the mixing time is O⁡(log3⁡n)O(\log^{3}n).

Tmix=min⁡{n:‖pn​(x,⋅)−𝒰‖≤14​ for all x∈V},T_{\rm mix}=\min\{n:||p^{n}(x,\,\cdot)-{\cal U}||\leq{\textstyle{1\over 4}}\mbox{ for all $x\in V$}\}\,, (1)

where 𝒰{\cal U} denotes the uniform distribution.

For a probability distribution {pi:i∈V}\{p_{i}:i\in V\}, define the (relative) entropy of pp by ENT⁡(p)=∑i∈Vpi​log⁡(|V|​pi){\rm\sc ENT}(p)=\sum_{i\in V}p_{i}\log(|V|p_{i}), where we define 0​log⁡0=00\log 0=0. The following well-known inequality links relative entropy to total variation distance. We have

‖p−𝒰‖≤12​ENT​(p).||p-{\cal U}||\leq\sqrt{{\textstyle{1\over 2}}{\rm\sc ENT}(p)}. (2)

If XX is a random variable (or random permutation) taking finitely many values, define ENT⁡(X){\rm\sc ENT}(X) as the relative entropy of the distribution of XX. Note that if 𝐏⁡(X=i)=pi{\bf P}(X=i)=p_{i} for i∈Vi\in V then ENT⁡(X)=𝐄⁡(log⁡(|V|​pX)){\rm\sc ENT}(X)={\bf{E}}(\log(|V|p_{X})). We shall think of the distribution of a random permutation in 𝒮n{\cal S}_{n} as a sequence of probabilities of length n!n!, indexed by permutations in 𝒮n{\cal S}_{n}. If ℱ{\cal F} is a sigma-field, then we shall write ENT⁡(X|ℱ){\rm\sc ENT}(X{\,|\,}{\cal F}) for the relative entropy of the conditional distribution of XX given ℱ{\cal F}. Note that ENT⁡(X|ℱ){\rm\sc ENT}(X{\,|\,}{\cal F}) is a random variable. If π\pi is a random permutation in SnS_{n}, then for 1≤k≤n1\leq k\leq n, define ℱk=σ⁡(π−1​(k),…,π−1​(n)){\cal F}_{k}=\sigma(\pi^{-1}(k),\dots,\pi^{-1}(n)), and define ENT⁡(π,k)=ENT⁡(π−1​(k)|ℱk+1){\rm\sc ENT}(\pi,k)={\rm\sc ENT}(\pi^{-1}(k){\,|\,}{\cal F}_{k+1}) (where we think of the conditional distribution of π−1​(k)\pi^{-1}(k) given ℱk+1{\cal F}_{k+1} as being a sequence of length kk). The standard entropy chain rule (see, e.g., [2]) gives the following proposition.

Proposition 1

For any i≤ni\leq n we have

ENT⁡(π)=𝐄⁡(ENT⁡(π|ℱi))+∑k=in𝐄⁡(ENT⁡(π,k)).{\rm\sc ENT}(\pi)={\bf{E}}\Bigl({\rm\sc ENT}(\pi{\,|\,}{\cal F}_{i})\Bigr)+\sum_{k=i}^{n}{\bf{E}}({\rm\sc ENT}(\pi,k)).

To compute the relative entropy in first term on the right hand side, we think of the distribution of π\pi given ℱi{\cal F}_{i} as a sequence of probabilities of length (i−1)!(i-1)!.

Remark: Substituting i=1i=1 into the formula gives ENT⁡(π)=∑k=1n𝐄⁡(ENT⁡(π,k)){\rm\sc ENT}(\pi)=\sum_{k=1}^{n}{\bf{E}}({\rm\sc ENT}(\pi,k)).

Proposition 4

([6]) Fix p≥0p\geq 0. The function d⁡(p,⋅)d(p,\,\cdot) is convex.

Lemma 6

d⁡(μ,𝒰)≥clog⁡|V|​ENT​(μ),d(\mu,{\cal U})\geq{c\over\log|V|}{\rm\sc ENT}(\mu),

A card shuffle can be described as a random permutation chosen from a certain probability distribution. If we start with the identity permutation and each shuffle has the distribution of π\pi, then after tt steps the cards are distributed like π1⋯πt\pi_{1}\cdots\pi_{t}, where the πi\pi_{i} are i.i.d. copies of π\pi.

4 Thorp shuffle

Recall that the Thorp shuffle has the following description. Assume that the number of cards, nn, is even. Cut the deck into two equal piles. Drop the first card from the left pile or the right pile according to the outcome of a fair coin flip; then drop from the other pile. Continue this way, with independent coin flips deciding whether to drop left-right or right-left each time, until both piles are empty.

We will actually work with the time reversal of the Thorp shuffle, which has the same mixing time (since the Thorp shuffle is a random walk on a group; see [12]). For convenience, we assume that n=2dn=2^{d} is a power of two. By writing the position of each card, from the bottom card (00) to the top card (2d−12^{d}-1), in binary, we can view the positions as elements of the dd-dimensional unit hypercube {0,1}d\{0,1\}^{d}. The reverse Thorp (RT) shuffle can then be constructed in the following way (see, e.g., [9]). Let Z={Z(l,t):l∈{0,1}d−1,t∈{0,1,…}}Z=\Bigl\{Z(l,t):l\in\{0,1\}^{d-1},t\in\{0,1,\dots\}\Bigr\} be a collection of i.i.d., Bernoulli(1/2) random variables. Note that x∈{0,1}dx\in\{0,1\}^{d} can be written as x=(L⁡(x),R⁡(x))x=(L(x),R(x)), where L⁡(x)L(x) and R⁡(x)R(x) are the leftmost d−1d-1 and rightmost bit, respectively, of xx. The transition rule for the RT shuffle is as follows. At time tt, suppose that the current state Xt=πX_{t}=\pi. Then the new state Xt+1=ν∘πX_{t+1}=\nu\circ\pi, where ν\nu is the permutation that sends

(L,R)→(R⊕Z⁡(L,t),L).(L,R)\to(R\oplus Z(L,t),L).

We are now ready to state the technical result of this paper.

Lemma 7

Let XtX_{t} be the reverse Thorp shuffle with 2d2^{d} cards. There is a universal constant cc such that if μ\mu is a random permutation which is independent of {Xt}\{X_{t}\} then

ENT⁡(Xd∘μ)≤(1−c/d)​ENT​(μ).{\rm\sc ENT}(X_{d}\circ\mu)\leq(1-c/d){\rm\sc ENT}(\mu).
